title: Time Converter
context: Grade 3, the second half of the time chapter. An adult sees sums with 60 and 24 in them. What is actually being settled is what those two numbers are: sixty small steps in an hour and twenty-four hours in a day, and that a length of time is a stretch laid along a clock, which has to be counted in two pieces when it crosses noon. A child who learned the rule alone will multiply by 60 for days, or subtract 10 from 3 for a match that runs from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.

writeup.why: Change hours into minutes and days into hours with an hour filling and a day turning, find how long something takes by laying a bar along a day strip through noon, and find when something ends by sliding the bar.
writeup.look: A wall clock and a stopwatch at the left with a row of twelve five-minute tiles under them, a day strip of twenty-four hour tiles along the foot with a green bar laid on it, a column board, and on the third phase a row of six small clocks.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Time Converter' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the minutes, hours or days now on the stage. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The real wall clock is 280 across at x 90, y 230, with its twelve numbers, sixty minute marks and its vermilion hour hand and deep blue minute hand, drawn exactly. The real stopwatch is a round brass face 130 across at x 400, y 240 with a start button on top. The row of twelve five-minute tiles runs at x 400, y 400, each tile 44 by 60 with a 6 gap, empty until the minute hand is dragged round, and labelled 5, 10 and on to 60 as it fills, with the words one hour at its end. The train ticket card or the calendar page card stands at x 690, y 232, 320 by 150, drawn as a real ticket or a real calendar page with its words and numbers. The day strip runs along the foot at x 90, y 610, twenty-four tiles each 40 by 50 with no gap, the first twelve sky blue and labelled a.m. and the next twelve amber and labelled p.m., with a notch and the words 12 noon between them and the words 12 midnight at both ends. The green bar is 40 tall at y 548, laid by dragging its two ends, and it is drawn in two pieces with their two lengths written above when it crosses noon. The column board stands at x 780, y 400, 240 by 150, an hours column and a minutes column with a carry slot above each. On the third phase six small clocks, each 100 across, stand in a row at x 90, y 240 in place of the wall clock, each with a tag that reads minutes after the start. On the fourth phase the flight card or the school bell card stands in the place of the ticket. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys, a colon key and two keys labelled a.m. and p.m., for typing a count of minutes, hours or days or a time with a.m. or p.m. into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours. The hour hand of a clock is vermilion and the minute hand is deep blue, because a hand is a mark that stands for a number, and the hours are vermilion and the minutes deep blue everywhere else, in a digital time, a label and a tag. The a.m. half of a day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber. The time reached, a length of time worked out, a converted amount and the answer are green. A clock face, rim and numbers are near-black on cream, anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey, and chrome never borrows one of the five. Each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a time is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The wall clock, the day strip and the bar show the last length of time or end time, with the hour in vermilion, the minutes in deep blue, the a.m. half sky blue, the p.m. half amber and the answer green.

phases.win: the twelfth tile fills, the row reads one hour, and the answer tag turns green
phases.does: drags the minute hand once round, watches the tiles fill to sixty, then types the minutes in the journey
phases.goal: one hour is sixty minutes, so hours change into minutes by multiplying by sixty
phases.says: One round of the minute hand fills an hour. How many minutes are in it?
phases.check: Away from the screen: turn a paper plate clock once round. How many minutes did the minute hand cover? Then turn it three times.
phases.feels: the minute hand sweeping round and the twelve tiles ticking full one after another
phases.hands: Time one minute with a stopwatch while the class claps, then turn a paper plate clock once round and say how many minutes that is.
phases.tries: First rung: how many minutes in one hour. Second rung: how many hours are in the journey, and how many minutes is each. Third rung: the same task with a journey of only whole hours, before the minutes come back.

writeup.delight: Two small surprises. On the first phase, as the minute hand sweeps round, each five-minute tile fills with a small tick of the stopwatch and the last tile closes the row with the stopwatch button popping up. On the third and fourth phases, the green bar crosses noon and splits into two pieces that slide together into one total, and slid backwards they split again.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet typed. On the first phase the wall clock stands with both hands at twelve, the row of twelve five-minute tiles is empty, and a train ticket card names a journey of some hours and minutes. On the second the day wheel stands with its sky blue half and its amber half and a calendar page card names a holiday of some days. On the third the day strip carries a start and an end across noon, a green bar waits beside it, and a row of six small clocks stands ready. On the fourth the green bar of the time taken waits at the start of the strip and a flight or a school bell card names the start. One thing moves, once: the minute hand, the wheel or the bar gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any count of hours, minutes or days on the clock and the wheel, the green bar slid along the day strip, and the column board. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on choosing minutes or hours, days into hours, a class that ends at noon, a lunch break, bottles filled in a minute, a night's sleep in a day, a school race on a stopwatch and when a school bell rings, each on a real thing.
voiceLines: A clock, a stopwatch and a day strip. Let us count the time.
One round of the minute hand fills an hour. How many minutes are in it?
The wheel turns once for one day. How many hours is that? Now for each day.
Lay the bar from the start to the end. Count to noon, then on from noon.
Slide the bar from the start. Add the hours first. Then the minutes. Which side of noon is it?
A new time to work out. What is it about?
Free play. Fill an hour, turn a day and slide the bar as you like.
Count again, one step at a time. Which side of noon are you on?
You counted the time with the hour filling and the day turning.

observations.why: the minute hand moves five minutes from one number to the next, and twelve fives make sixty.
observations.soWhat: an hour is sixty minutes, so hours change into minutes by multiplying by sixty.
observations.observe: One round of the minute hand filled twelve five-minute tiles and the row read sixty.

observations.why: the hour hand goes round twice in a day, once for the a.m. half and once for the p.m. half.
observations.soWhat: a day is twenty-four hours, so days change into hours by multiplying by twenty-four.
observations.observe: The day wheel turned once and counted twenty-four hour tiles, twelve sky blue and twelve amber.

observations.why: the day strip has a notch at noon, and the part before it and the part after it are counted apart.
observations.soWhat: to find how long something takes across noon, count to noon and from noon, and add.
observations.observe: A bar that crossed noon split into two pieces and the two lengths added up to the whole.

observations.why: the bar is as long as the time taken, so its end is the start plus that time.
observations.soWhat: to find when something ends, add the time taken to the start time, hours first and then minutes.
observations.observe: Sliding the bar from the start put its end on the time the thing finishes.

serves.exercise: choosing minutes or hours for each of six activities
changing hours and days into minutes and hours in six pairs
ticking the sensible length of time for five things
changing three hours thirty minutes into minutes
finding how long a nursery class lasts from nine in the morning to half past eleven
finding the total hours of a train journey of two days twenty-two hours
finding when the bell rings from a start time, a journey and an early arrival
answering four questions about the finishing times of six honey eating bears
finding how long one minute is by writing, clapping and filling bottles

source_tool.description: A real wall clock, 280 across, stands at the left of the working area, with its twelve numbers, sixty minute marks and an hour hand and a minute hand, the hour hand vermilion and the minute hand deep blue. Beside it stands a real stopwatch with a round face and a start button. A row of twelve five-minute tiles runs under them, each tile 44 across. When the minute hand is dragged once round the clock the tiles fill one at a time, labelled 5, 10 and on to 60, until the row reads sixty minutes and a small label says one hour. Along the foot of the working area runs a day strip of twenty-four hour tiles, the first twelve sky blue and labelled a.m., the next twelve amber and labelled p.m., with a notch and the words 12 noon between them. A green bar the child sets by dragging its two ends is laid along the strip to show a length of time, and it is drawn in two pieces, with the two lengths written above them, when it crosses noon. Sliding the whole bar along the strip moves its end. A column board with an hours column and a minutes column takes a sum, with a carry shown above the column it joins. On the third phase a row of six small clocks, each reading a finishing time as minutes after a start, replaces the wall clock, and the child taps the longest and the shortest. A number pad sets any count and types any answer. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many minutes, hours or days are on the stage.
source_tool.art_direction: A classroom wall with a clock and stopwatch / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Real everyday objects, drawn as recognisable flat illustrations that a child knows at a glance: a wall clock with its numbers, a wristwatch, a digital alarm clock, a school bell, a stopwatch, a sunrise over a school, a street lamp at night, a wall calendar page, a birthday card, a football, a film ticket. The object is the thing the child reads or sets, and a plain dial or a bare number appears only as a second view the child can switch to.

Every clock is drawn exactly: twelve numbers, sixty minute marks with a longer mark at every fifth, the minute hand turning six degrees a minute and the hour hand thirty degrees an hour plus half a degree a minute, so the hour hand sits between two numbers whenever the minutes are not zero. Neither hand has an arrowhead, and the two hands never lie on top of each other in a picture that asks the child to read them.
A time is always written the way it is said: 7:20, quarter past 7, 7:20 a.m. A.m. and p.m. are written with the time and never alone, and noon and midnight are never given an a.m. or a p.m.

A length of time is drawn as a bar or a band laid along a clock or a day strip from its start to its end, so the child sees how long, and a band that crosses noon is drawn through the noon mark in two pieces.
A date is written in boxes: a day box, a month box and a year box, and a day is never written without its month and year.
A calendar page is a grid of seven columns headed with the days of the week, Sunday first, and its first day starts in the right column.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a number or a day the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a wall clock keeps its frame and a school bell stays brass. The hour hand of a clock is vermilion and the minute hand is deep blue, because a hand is a mark that stands for a number, on a clock whose face, rim and numbers are near-black on cream, and the hours are vermilion and the minutes deep blue everywhere else, in a digital time, a label and a tag. The a.m. half of a day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue, and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber. The time reached, a length of time worked out, a converted amount and the answer are green. Those five are the same five in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Hour hand, Minute hand, a.m., p.m. and Answer, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Count again, one step at a time. Which side of noon are you on?
voice.onNext: A new time to work out. What is it about?
voice.opening: A clock, a stopwatch and a day strip. Let us count the time.
voice.onFinish: You counted the time with the hour filling and the day turning.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Fill an hour, turn a day and slide the bar as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has timed one minute with a stopwatch, writing or clapping, and has sat a paper plate clock at the start and the end of a lesson. The tool is what fills an hour with sixty marks and lays a length of time along a whole day, which a paper plate cannot do in front of the child.

answer_key.rule: There are 60 minutes in an hour, so hours change into minutes by multiplying by 60, and an hour and some minutes is changed by changing the hours and adding the minutes. There are 24 hours in a day, so days change into hours by multiplying by 24. To find how long something takes, count from the start to noon and from noon to the end, and add the two parts; if it does not cross noon, count straight across. To find when something ends, add the time taken to the start time, hours first and then minutes, and write a.m. or p.m. by which side of noon the end falls on. Noon and midnight take neither a.m. nor p.m.
answer_key.wrong: The hour fills again slowly, one five-minute tile at a time, or the bar is laid along the day strip again and cut at noon into its two pieces, and the pieces are counted aloud. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Change the hours first: 9 hours is 540 minutes.
Then add the 10 minutes. 540 plus 10 is 550.
items.question: A train ticket shows a journey of 9 hours 10 minutes. How many minutes is that?
items.checkpoint: Change the hours into minutes first, then add the minutes.
items.misconception: Writing 910 by joining the 9 and the 10, or forgetting to change the hours at all.

items.question: A calendar page shows a holiday that lasts 8 days. How many hours is that?
items.checkpoint: A day has 24 hours, so multiply the days by 24.
items.misconception: Multiplying by 60, the minutes in an hour, because the last answer was done with 60.

steps: Count from 10 a.m. to 12 noon: 2 hours.
Then count from 12 noon to 3 p.m.: 3 hours.
Add the two parts: 2 plus 3 is 5.
So from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. is 5 hours.
items.question: A cricket match starts at 10 a.m. and ends at 3 p.m. How long does the match last?
items.checkpoint: Count to noon first, then on from noon, and add the two parts.
items.misconception: Taking 10 from 3, or counting 3 minus 10 as if the clock never passed noon.

steps: Add the hours first: 9:20 a.m. plus 3 hours is 12:20 p.m.
Then add the 45 minutes: 12:20 p.m. plus 45 minutes is 1:05 p.m.
The time passed noon, so it is p.m.
So the flight lands at 1:05 p.m.
items.question: A flight leaves at 9:20 a.m. and takes 3 hours 45 minutes. When does the flight land?
items.checkpoint: Add the hours first, then the minutes, and say a.m. or p.m. by which side of noon it is.
items.misconception: Writing 12:65 for the minutes, or keeping a.m. after the time has passed noon.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A child brushes teeth with a toothbrush and then sleeps in a bed all night. Which unit fits brushing teeth, minutes or hours? Which unit fits a night's sleep?
items.final_answer: Minutes fit brushing teeth, and hours fit a night's sleep

items.question: A bus tour on a calendar page lasts 10 days. How many hours is that?
items.final_answer: 240 hours, because 1 day is 24 hours and 10 times 24 is 240

items.question: A story class starts at 11 a.m. and ends at 12 noon. How long is the class?
items.final_answer: 1 hour, because from 11 a.m. to 12 noon is 1 hour

items.question: The school bell rings for lunch at 12 noon. Lunch lasts 1 hour. When does lunch end?
items.final_answer: 1 p.m., because 12 noon plus 1 hour is 1 p.m.

items.question: A child fills 3 bottles with a mug in 1 minute, timed on a stopwatch. How many bottles can the child fill in 1 hour at the same speed?
items.final_answer: 180 bottles, because 1 hour is 60 minutes and 3 times 60 is 180

items.question: A child sleeps in a bed for 9 hours each night. A day has 24 hours. How many hours of the day is the child awake?
Two children start a pot painting race at 12 noon and a stopwatch times them. The first stops at 12:25 p.m. and the second stops at 1:05 p.m. How much longer did the second child take?
items.final_answer: 40 minutes longer. From 12 noon to 12:25 p.m. is 25 minutes, and from 12 noon to 1:05 p.m. is 65 minutes

items.question: A child leaves home at 7:20 a.m. and takes 25 minutes to walk to school. The child reaches the gate 10 minutes before the school bell rings. When does the bell ring?
items.final_answer: 7:55 a.m., because 7:20 a.m. plus 25 minutes is 7:45 a.m., and the bell rings 10 minutes later

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: drags once round the wall clock, and the five-minute tiles fill one at a time
turns once through the twenty-four hour tiles, the a.m. half sky blue and the p.m. half amber
drag to lay a green bar along the day strip from a start to an end
moves the whole bar along the strip so its end shows when something ends
takes a sum of hours and minutes with the carry shown above the column
shows six small clocks as minutes after a start, and the child taps the longest and the shortest
types any count of hours, minutes or days and any answer

teaching_notes: Time one minute with a stopwatch before the tool opens: write the school name, clap, or fill bottles with a mug and a funnel, and count. Say that an hour is sixty of those minutes, and let a paper plate clock turn once to show it. Lay a long paper strip marked in twenty-four hours with noon in the middle, colour the morning half sky blue and the evening half amber, and lay a strip of card along it from a start to an end. When the card crosses noon, cut it there and add the two pieces, and wait for the child to say why before you show the rule. Write noon as 12 noon and midnight as 12 midnight, and never give either of them a.m. or p.m. Use fresh times: the exercise's shifts, films and practice sessions are the child's own to work.
generation_prompt: Build a time conversion tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage, drawn from real everyday objects as recognisable flat illustrations in their natural colours, with no photographs and no people. A real wall clock, 280 across, stands at the left of the working area with twelve numbers, sixty minute marks, a vermilion hour hand and a deep blue minute hand, and a real stopwatch stands beside it. A row of twelve five-minute tiles runs under them and fills one tile at a time as the minute hand is dragged once round, until it reads sixty minutes. A day strip of twenty-four hour tiles runs along the foot, the first twelve sky blue and labelled a.m., the next twelve amber and labelled p.m., noon notched between them. A green bar with two draggable ends is laid along the strip to show a length of time, and is drawn in two pieces with their two lengths written above them when it crosses noon, and the whole bar slides along the strip to show an end time. A column board with an hours column and a minutes column takes sums with the carry shown above the column it joins. On the third phase a row of six small clocks reading minutes after a start replaces the wall clock and the child taps the longest and the shortest. A number pad types counts and answers. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the minutes, hours or days on the stage. Noon and midnight never carry a.m. or p.m. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Fill the hour with sixty minutes. Turn the day wheel. Lay the green bar along the day. Slide it to find when it ends.
